claims.claim: MLA compresses a standard-MHA KV cache from 327–516 KB/token to 70 KB/token, a 4.66–7.28x reduction.

evidence.observation: The paper gives cache elements/token as 2*n_h*d_h*l for MHA and (d_c+d_h^R)*l, approximately 4.5*d_h*l, for MLA, with d_c=4*d_h and d_h^R=d_h/2. It does not report these KB/token endpoints or ratios; for the stated n_h=128, the formula ratio is about 56.9x in equal-width elements, not 4.66–7.28x.

claims.claim: FlashMLA's four variants include dense MLA prefill on SM100 alongside dense/sparse MLA decoding and sparse MLA prefill.

evidence.locator: support matrix and Dense MHA Prefill usage section
evidence.observation: The repository classifies dense prefill on SM100 as MHA with d_qk 192/128 and d_v 128, not MLA/MQA; dense and sparse decode plus sparse prefill are MLA-mode MQA paths.

claims.claim: Every MLA KV-cache token is a 656-byte entry containing 512 FP8 bytes, 16 bytes of per-head FP32 scales, and 128 BF16 RoPE bytes, with 64-token dense pages and variable sparse pages.

evidence.observation: The 656-byte layout is specifically DeepSeek V3/V3.1/V3.2 FP8+sparse decode; dense decode uses BF16. Its four FP32 scales are per 128-value group within each token, not per head. page_block_size is an input shape rather than a universal dense/sparse page rule.
The repository also implements a distinct 512-dimensional MODEL1_FP8Sparse format with seven E8M0 scales, disproving a universal 656-byte MLA layout.

claims.claim: Dense MLA decode uses a fixed 64-token page and reaches up to 3000 GB/s memory-bound and 660 TFLOPS compute-bound on H800.

evidence.observation: The 3000-GB/s and 660-TFLOPS author-reported maxima on H800 SXM5/CUDA 12.8 are exact, but the public interface accepts page_block_size from the KV tensor and does not specify a fixed value of 64; 64 is a test default.

claims.claim: The displayed dense-decode CUDA template is a faithful SM90 BF16 FlashMLA structure using an FP8 cache, explicit scale/RoPE arrays, TMA, and one warpgroup per query head.

evidence.locator: dense and sparse_fp8 implementations plus public interface
evidence.observation: The snippet is not upstream code and mixes mutually exclusive modes: dense decode is BF16, while FP8 cache dispatch is sparse; the real implementation uses generated/specialized kernels, scheduler metadata, separate split/combine paths, and different tensor contracts.

claims.claim: Sparse MLA consumes token indices and computes attention only over the specified tokens.

evidence.locator: Sparse Attention indices contract and sparse-prefill equivalence
evidence.observation: Decode indices encode selected page/offset entries and sparse prefill gathers focused_kv=kv[indices] before QK and PV operations.

challenge.alternative: The indices merely mask scores after all KV entries have already been read.
challenge.check: Trace the decode index-to-address logic and sparse-prefill reference gather.
challenge.outcome: The SM90/SM100 kernels derive KV addresses from supplied indices, and the reference computation gathers only selected KV rows; this is not a post-read dense mask.

claims.claim: The displayed sparse CUDA template accurately represents FlashMLA's sparse API and its 656-byte cache retrieval.

evidence.observation: The invented template is not an upstream kernel. Decode takes page-encoded [batch,s_q,topk] indices and the 656-byte layout only in one FP8 mode; sparse prefill instead takes BF16 [s_kv,h_kv,d_qk] KV and [s_q,h_kv,topk] indices.

claims.claim: FlashMLA's SM100 dense MLA prefill uses tcgen05/TMEM for forward and backward and reaches 1460/1000 TFLOPS on B200; the displayed five-stage sketch describes that path.

evidence.locator: MHA prefill benchmark, support matrix, and Dense MHA Prefill section
evidence.observation: The 1460/1000 figures belong to NVIDIA's dense MHA forward/backward implementation, not an MLA-prefill variant. Pinned source does use TMEM/TMA in that MHA implementation, but the page's pseudocode is invented and supplies unverified role/dataflow details.

claims.claim: Dense MLA decode is author-reported at up to 660 TFLOPS and 3000 GB/s on H800, and the support matrix labels its cache BF16.

evidence.observation: The source states both maxima for H800 SXM5 with CUDA 12.8 and lists Dense Decoding / SM90 / MQA / BF16.

challenge.alternative: The 3000-GB/s and 660-TFLOPS figures describe one simultaneous operating point or an FP8 path.
challenge.check: Read the exact benchmark qualification and support row.
challenge.outcome: The source explicitly separates memory-bound and compute-bound configurations and labels dense-decode KV format BF16, so the table must preserve that distinction.

claims.claim: Sparse decode runs at 410 TFLOPS on H800 and up to 350 TFLOPS on B200 with dtype FP8.

evidence.observation: The values are exact author reports, but FP8 describes the KV-cache storage; the source explicitly says matrix multiplication is bfloat16. A single Dtype=FP8 column materially obscures the compute precision.

claims.claim: Dense prefill forward and backward are author-reported at up to 1460 and 1000 TFLOPS on B200 with BF16 tensors.

evidence.locator: dense MHA prefill performance and support matrix
evidence.observation: The repository transcribes NVIDIA's B200 maxima and its test/API use BF16 Q/K/V. The rows are MHA prefill, not MLA decode.

challenge.alternative: The figures are MLA prefill results or independently reproduced DeepSeek benchmarks.
challenge.check: Compare the benchmark heading, news entry, support matrix, and test name.
challenge.outcome: Every locator calls this dense MHA on SM100 and attributes the numbers to NVIDIA, excluding an MLA or reproduced interpretation.

claims.claim: Sparse prefill reaches up to 640 TFLOPS on H800 and 1450 TFLOPS on B200 with dtype FP8.

evidence.locator: sparse MLA prefill performance, API contract, and equivalent PyTorch code
evidence.observation: The values and H800 CUDA 12.8/B200 CUDA 12.9 environments are source-reported, but sparse-prefill Q and KV tensors are explicitly bfloat16; the source does not label this path FP8.

claims.claim: FlashMLA powers the DeepSeek-V3 and DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp model families.

evidence.observation: The first-party repository explicitly says its optimized attention kernels power DeepSeek-V3 and DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp.

challenge.alternative: The repository is only a standalone benchmark and is not connected to model deployments.
challenge.check: Compare the first-party introduction and sparse-kernel release note with the linked model repositories.
challenge.outcome: Both identify the kernels as powering the named model families and DSA release, although no broader serving-stack claim follows.

claims.claim: SGLang and vLLM provide day-0 FlashMLA support.

evidence.observation: The related vLLM source is a 2026 warning about FP8 prefill query quantization, not evidence of launch-day FlashMLA support; the FlashInfer PR is likewise a separate PDL change, and no SGLang source is attached. The unversioned 'day-0' statement is therefore a misleading source conflation.

claims.claim: CUTLASS has SM100 MLA attention kernels with a separate fused-reduction implementation.

evidence.observation: Example 77 adds the SM100 MLA-shape backward path and includes kernel/sm100_fmha_mla_reduction.hpp; PR 2472 separately captures forward MLA shape support.

challenge.alternative: The reduction is merely generic FMHA code and no MLA specialization exists.
challenge.check: Inspect the pinned PR paths and the d_qk=192/d_vo=128 specialization descriptions.
challenge.outcome: The exact file and surrounding device/kernel paths are MLA-named and tied to the asymmetric MLA shape, distinguishing them from generic FMHA.

claims.claim: FlashMLA sparse prefill/decode kernels power DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp's token-level DSA/NSA path and are applicable to long-sequence sparse attention.

evidence.observation: The repository identifies token-level sparse prefill and decode kernels as powering DeepSeek Sparse Attention in DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp.

challenge.alternative: The sparse kernels are generic pruning utilities unrelated to the released model's attention execution.
challenge.check: Follow the first-party DSA release statement and API descriptions.
challenge.outcome: The repository explicitly connects both sparse attention stages to DSA and exposes attention operators that consume selected-token indices.

claims.claim: FlashMLA is relevant to serving DeepSeek MLA models and to decode workloads where KV-cache footprint or bandwidth is limiting.

evidence.observation: MLA reduces per-token KV elements via low-rank latent caching.
The library targets DeepSeek models and reports a memory-bound dense-decode regime, supporting the stated selection context without promising a speedup.

challenge.alternative: KV compression is only a model-storage property and has no bearing on the decode kernel choice.
challenge.check: Compare the MLA cache formula with FlashMLA's separately reported memory-bound decode benchmark and model linkage.
challenge.outcome: The cache is an input to the paged decode operator and the source explicitly measures a bandwidth-bound regime; this supports relevance, not universal superiority.

claims.claim: The 656-byte latent KV-cache format is generally tied to DeepSeek's MLA architecture.

evidence.locator: DeepSeek V3/V3.1/V3.2 FP8+sparse docstring and dispatch
evidence.observation: 656 bytes is tied to one V3-family FP8+sparse decode mode, not MLA generally: dense decode is BF16 and another sparse model layout is 512-dimensional with a different scale representation.

claims.claim: FlashMLA's dense prefill support is SM100-only.

evidence.observation: Dense Prefill is listed only for SM100 and in MHA mode.

challenge.alternative: SM90 dense prefill exists elsewhere in the tree or is implied by global SM90 support.
challenge.check: Compare the support matrix with setup.py source lists and public prefill API dispatch.
challenge.outcome: Dense-prefill build sources and dispatch are under sm100, while SM90 support applies to decode and sparse prefill, not this dense MHA path.

claims.claim: Sparse MLA needs selected-token indices from an indexing stage outside the FlashMLA attention operator.

evidence.observation: Both sparse APIs receive caller-produced int32 indices; no top-k selector is invoked by the attention interfaces.

challenge.alternative: FlashMLA computes top-k internally before attention.
challenge.check: Trace public signatures, extension calls, and index address use.
challenge.outcome: Indices are required inputs passed into sparse_decode_fwd/sparse_prefill_fwd and directly control gathers; the library code audited here does not produce them.

claims.claim: The FlashMLA GitHub link and DeepSeek-V3 technical report are relevant first-party sources.

evidence.observation: This is the first-party implementation snapshot audited.
This is the named model's first-party technical report and provides model-level MLA context.

challenge.alternative: The links refer to unrelated implementations or secondary summaries.
challenge.check: Resolve authorship, repository owner, and paper title/model identity.
challenge.outcome: Both are DeepSeek-authored primary sources for the implementation or model context.

claims.claim: The CUTLASS SM100 attention changelog is relevant to the adjacent SM100 MLA implementation.

evidence.observation: The version-pinned primary PR adds Example 77's SM100 MLA forward implementation; it is stronger and more stable evidence than the mutable latest changelog URL.

challenge.alternative: CUTLASS material is the DeepSeek FlashMLA implementation itself.
challenge.outcome: It is a separate adjacent NVIDIA implementation of an MLA-shaped prefill kernel, relevant only when explicitly labeled as such.

claims.claim: The full artifact directory is a verbatim upstream FlashMLA implementation and its derived variant accurately represents FlashMLA decode.

evidence.observation: The two files come from separate NVIDIA CUTLASS and FlashInfer repositories, not deepseek-ai/FlashMLA; the bundle-level origin records only CUTLASS.
The fragment uses a false Dc=128 assumption and conflates SM90 wgmma with SM100 tcgen05, so it is not a faithful FlashMLA decode reference.

claims.claim: The displayed get_page command returns the FlashMLA page and included code artifacts.

evidence.command: conda run -n base python scripts/get_page.py kernel-flashmla --include-code
evidence.result: Command exits successfully and returns the page plus both full and derived artifact sections.
evidence.negative_control: Changing the ID to kernel-flashmla-does-not-exist exits nonzero with 'Page not found'.

challenge.alternative: The command is stale, requires bare python3, or omits the referenced artifact bundle.
challenge.check: Execute it in the required conda environment and repeat with a known-absent page ID.
challenge.outcome: The real ID resolves and includes artifacts; the false ID fails, discriminating actual page lookup.

claims.claim: Structured B200 performance records support 1460 TFLOPS BF16 dense prefill and 1450 TFLOPS FP8 sparse prefill at approximately 65% utilization for the listed shapes.

evidence.observation: The repository reports the two throughput maxima but no ~65% utilization and no complete shape/timing record. Dense prefill is MHA; sparse prefill's documented inputs are BF16 rather than FP8. These omissions and dtype error make both structured records inadmissible.
